subject: Accounting
title: WorldCom's $11 Billion Lie
description: A 60-second lesson on WorldCom's $11 Billion Lie.

hook.text: WorldCom turned operating expenses into capital assets with a few journal entries. $11 billion worth.

buildup.text: Line costs—the fees WorldCom paid to use other networks—were its biggest operating expense.

discovery.text: By reclassifying expenses as assets, WorldCom inflated profits and hid its real financial state.

twist.text: The fraud was discovered by an internal auditor, Cynthia Cooper, working nights to avoid detection.

climax.text: WorldCom filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history at the time—$107 billion in assets.

punchline.text: One reclassification. Eleven billion in fraud.

details.summary: WorldCom committed the largest accounting fraud in US history at the time by capitalizing $11 billion in ordinary operating expenses to inflate profits. This topic covers the mechanics of the fraud, how internal auditor Cynthia Cooper uncovered it, and the aftermath.
details.whyItMatters: WorldCom's fraud was shockingly simple—reclassifying expenses as capital expenditures. Its discovery by an internal auditor, not the external firm, highlights the critical importance of internal audit independence.
takeaways: WorldCom reclassified $11 billion in line costs from operating expenses to capital assets
This simple reclassification converted billions in losses into apparent profits
Internal auditor Cynthia Cooper discovered the fraud by conducting an unauthorized investigation

faq.question: How did WorldCom commit its $11 billion fraud?
faq.answer: WorldCom reclassified ordinary operating expenses—mainly line costs paid to other telecom carriers—as capital expenditures. This moved them from the income statement to the balance sheet, instantly converting what should have been losses into reported profits.

faq.question: How was the WorldCom fraud discovered?
faq.answer: VP of Internal Audit Cynthia Cooper and her small team discovered the fraud by conducting their own investigation, often working at night to avoid detection by management. She reported findings directly to the audit committee, bypassing the CFO who was orchestrating the fraud.
